items.title: 6.2.4 Position of a Point with Respect to a Circle

source_refs.note: Book p. 176: 6.2.4 Theorem 1 (outside, on, inside) with Proof and Figure 6.8; Example 11

blocks.text:
Theorem 1: The point \(P(x_{1}, y_{1})\) lies outside, on, or inside the circle
\[x^{2} + y^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0\]
according as
\[x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2} + 2gx_{1} + 2fy_{1} + c \gtreqless 0\]

blocks.alt: On a pale yellow panel, a magenta circle with centre C(-g, -f) and three points P(x1, y1) joined to the centre by cyan segments: one outside the circle (upper left), one on the circle (right) and one inside it (below the centre).
blocks.caption: Figure 6.8: A point P(x1, y1) outside, on and inside the circle with centre C(-g, -f) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.8)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The symbol \(\gtreqless\) is read in order: \(>\) goes with "outside", \(=\) with "on" and \(<\) with "inside". So one line of the theorem says three things at once.

Proof: The centre of the circle is \(C(-g, -f)\) and radius is \(r = \sqrt{g^{2} + f^{2} - c}\). The point \(P(x_{1}, y_{1})\) lies outside, on, or inside the circle according as
\[|CP| > r, \quad |CP| = r, \quad \text{or} \quad |CP| < r,\]
that is \(|CP| \gtreqless r\), that is, according as:
\[\sqrt{(x_{1} + g)^{2} + (y_{1} + f)^{2}} \gtreqless \sqrt{g^{2} + f^{2} - c}\]
Squaring both sides (since all quantities are non-negative):
\[(x_{1} + g)^{2} + (y_{1} + f)^{2} \gtreqless g^{2} + f^{2} - c\]
\[x_{1}^{2} + 2gx_{1} + g^{2} + y_{1}^{2} + 2fy_{1} + f^{2}\]
\[\gtreqless g^{2} + f^{2} - c\]
Cancelling \(g^{2}\) and \(f^{2}\):
\[x_{1}^{2} + 2gx_{1} + y_{1}^{2} + 2fy_{1} \gtreqless -c\]
Thus:
\[x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2} + 2gx_{1} + 2fy_{1} + c \gtreqless 0\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Two small facts make the proof work:
1. We compare distances, and distances are never negative, so squaring both sides keeps each inequality the same way round.
2. After cancelling, the left side minus the right side is \(|CP|^{2} - r^{2}\). So the number \(S_{1} = x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2} + 2gx_{1} + 2fy_{1} + c\) is really \(|CP|^{2} - r^{2}\); its sign tells where \(P\) is.
The coefficients of \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) must be 1 before you substitute. For \(2x^{2} + 2y^{2} + \ldots\), divide by 2 first (dividing by a positive number does not change the sign anyway).

blocks.title: Example 11
blocks.problem: Determine whether the point \(P(2, 3)\) lies outside, on, or inside the circle: \(x^{2} + y^{2} + 2x - 3y - 10 = 0\)
steps:
Given: the point \(P(2, 3)\) and the circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} + 2x - 3y - 10 = 0\).
To find: whether \(P\) is outside, on or inside the circle.
Method: Theorem 1. Put the coordinates of \(P\) in the left-hand side of the circle's equation (coefficients of \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) are already 1) and look at the sign of the result.

Step 1: Substitute \(x = 2\) and \(y = 3\) into the left-hand side
\[(2)^{2} + (3)^{2} + 2(2) - 3(3) - 10\]
\[= 4 + 9 + 4 - 9 - 10\]
\[= -2 < 0\]
Why: by Theorem 1 the sign of \(x_{1}^{2} + y_{1}^{2} + 2gx_{1} + 2fy_{1} + c\) decides the position.

Step 2: Conclude
The value is negative, so the point lies inside the circle.
Why: negative means \(|CP|^{2} < r^{2}\), that is, \(P\) is nearer to the centre than the radius.

Check:
\(2g = 2\), \(2f = -3\), so the centre is \(C\left(-1, \frac{3}{2}\right)\) and
\[r^{2} = 1 + \dfrac{9}{4} + 10 = \dfrac{53}{4}\]
\[|CP|^{2} = 3^{2} + \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{45}{4}\]
\(\frac{45}{4} < \frac{53}{4}\), and the difference \(\frac{45}{4} - \frac{53}{4} = -2\) is exactly the value found in Step 1.
blocks.answer: \(4 + 9 + 4 - 9 - 10 = -2 < 0\); thus, the point \(P(2, 3)\) lies inside the circle.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Put \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) in the left side of the circle's equation (with \(x^{2}\), \(y^{2}\) coefficients 1).
2. Positive: outside. Zero: on the circle. Negative: inside.
3. The value equals \(|CP|^{2} - r^{2}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Mixing up the signs: positive means outside, not inside.
2. Substituting into an equation whose \(x^{2}\), \(y^{2}\) coefficients are negative (for example after moving terms). Write the circle as \(x^{2} + y^{2} + \ldots = 0\) first.
3. Arithmetic slips with negative coefficients such as \(-3y\).
